title: Naturelab: Physiological effect of combined zeitgeber on reward functioning of the mesolimbic system
summary:
In modern societies, people are constantly surrounded by highly palatable and calorie-rich foods. This environment can make it difficult to eat according to the body’s actual energy needs and may contribute to overweight and metabolic diseases. One behavior that plays an important role in this process is emotional eating, meaning eating in response to stress or emotions rather to physical hunger. Previous research suggests that stress-related hormones (such as cortisol) and signals related to food intake (such as insulin) may influence how the brain responds to rewarding foods. Environmental factors such as light and temperature also help regulate the body’s daily biological rhythm. However, it is still not well understood how these internal body signals and external environmental cues interact and whether they influence emotional eating, particularly in the evening when people may be more prone to overeating.

This study therefore investigates whether brain processes related to reward and eating behavior differ between the morning and the evening. In addition, the study examines whether aligning internal body rhythms (for example stress-related hormone patterns) with external environmental cues (such as light exposure and time spent in natural environments) can influence these processes and emotional eating behavior.

Participants will attend measurement sessions in both the morning and the evening to examine possible differences across the day. In addition, participants will be assigned to one of three groups: a 12-week nature-based intervention, an online intervention, or a control group. Measurements will be conducted before and after the intervention period. During these assessments, behavioral measures related to motivation and learning, questionnaire assessments of emotional eating, and biological markers will be collected.

interventions.name: Group 1 (30 participants) will function as control group. These participants will not receive any intervention. They will receive a manual for self-trained relaxation exercises at the end of the study.

Group 2 (30 participants) will undergo a weekly online relaxation intervention (indoors) for 12 weeks with the aim to restore diurnal cortisol levels without additional exposure to external zeitgebers (light/ temperature).

Group 3 (30 participants) will undergo a weekly outdoor relaxation exercise for 12 weeks
with the aim to restore diurnal cortisol levels in alignment with extern zeitgeber (temperature and light).

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
- Full capacity to give consent
- Ability to understand study procedures and willingness to comply with them and provide written informed consent
- Good German language skills
- Non-smoker (for the last 1 year not smoked more than 2 cigarettes per month)
- Self-reported emotional eating verified by specialised clinician
Exclusion criteria:
- Inability to attend the weekly relaxation exercises (e.g. medical or organisational reasons)
- Serious or unstable medical illness preventing to attend the testing days
- Current alcoholism or consistent substance abuse
- Current and history of major psychiatric illness as defined by the DSM-IV criteria including severe eating disorders that would prevent the participant from executing the tasks of the experiment or the relaxation exercises
- Medications that affect alertness (e.g., barbiturates, benzodiazepines, chloral hydrate, haloperidol, lithium, phenytoin, etc.) and any psychoactive drugs or anti-obesity agents including anti-diabetic medication that affects food intake behaviour
- Any medication affecting emotional eating behaviour (such as GLP-1-analogues or antipsychotic medication)
- Pregnancy
- Nursing women
- Any factors prohibiting MRI measurements
